title: Why Australian Financial Advice Practices Are Moving Toward Outsourced Paraplanning & CSO
excerpt: Across Australia, financial advice practices are facing a structural shift. While the demand for financial advice remains strong, the ability to consistently deliver that advice is...
author: Advice Lab
contentHtml:
Across Australia, financial advice practices are facing a structural shift. While the demand for financial advice remains strong, the ability to consistently deliver that advice is under pressure.

Increasingly, the constraint isn’t how many advisers a firm has. It’s how much operational work those advisers are doing.

Why Australian advice practices are struggling with capacity

Industry data from Rainmaker Information and ASIC shows a clear trend:

  • Adviser numbers have declined significantly, Australia ended 2025 with over 15,000 registered financial advisers.
  • Around 30% of advisers now operate under AFSLs with 10 or fewer advisers

Large institutions used to take on graduates and junior staff, placing them into paraplanning and CSO roles where they could learn and progress. Today, small practices are expected to do this themselves, often without having the time, people, or scale to manage it properly.

At the same time, adviser workloads have become more complex. While the natural response is often to hire more staff, the reality is that hiring alone is no longer a dependable fix.

According to ASIC, recent reforms have increased documentation, consent tracking, and compliance obligations across advice businesses. For smaller firms, this creates a compounding effect. Every new client doesn’t just generate revenue. It adds operational strain.

Where does capacity break in advice practices

This pressure becomes most visible during peak periods. EOFY, review cycles, and regulatory deadlines often lead to:

  • SOAs stacking up
  • Fee consents falling behind
  • Advisers stepping into administrative work just to keep things moving

At that point, growth stalls, not because demand slows, but because delivery can’t keep up. 

If advisers are spending weekends clearing documentation, the issue isn’t seasonal. It’s structural.

The real question is: How much non-advice operational work you are doing?

If you're spending weekends clearing SOAs or chasing paperwork, your capacity issue may be structural, not seasonal.

Why hiring more staff isn’t solving advice practice capacity problem

Hiring more staff feels like a logical response. But for many practices, it introduces a different set of risks. Industry publications like Professional Planner highlights ongoing workforce constraints outlined by FAAA:

  • Limited pipeline of experienced paraplanners
  • Rising onboarding and training cost for advisers
  • Ongoing disruption from staff turnover in small teams
More importantly, hiring locks in costs but the advise work doesn’t. Workload may fluctuate throughout the year, but salaries remain fixed. Which creates a mismatch:

  • Quiet months reduce utilisation
  • Peak periods still create bottlenecks
  • One resignation can disrupt the entire workflow 
This is why more firms are rethinking capacity not as a fixed asset, but as something that needs a flex.

Why advice practices are moving toward outsourcing

Instead of adding permanent headcount, more practices are changing how work flows through the business. Outsourced paraplanning and CSO support are a part of that model. This shift is a result of an operating decision and not a cost decision. Typical functions of outsourced paraplanning and CSO includes:
  • SOA and ROA preparation
  • Strategy modelling and research
  • Annual review documentation
  • Client onboarding and date updates
  • Fee consent tracking and implementation
When this work moves away from advisers, something important happens: Capacity becomes flexible.

Is outsourcing paraplanning and CSO work compliant in Australia?

When deciding to outsource this often is the first concern. According to ASIC guidelines:
The answer is 'Yes'. With the right structure in place, outsourcing can operate within regulatory expectations while improving delivery capacity.

Outsourcing is permitted, provided that firms maintain governance, supervision, and accountability. The responsibility of the advice, however, remains with the licenses.

What benefits do advice practices get by outsourcing

Advice practices that outsource paraplanning and CSO work typically see three shifts:
  • Advisers spend more time on client-facing revenue-generating work 
  • Non-advice operational work becomes systemized and consistent 
  • Costs begin to align with workload, rather than sit fixing against it
Practically, this leads to:
  • Faster turnaround during peak periods
  • Reduced burnout and fewer errors
  • More predictable margins
  • A more consistent client experience

And, most importantly, it protects the adviser's energy, which is finite.

If you’re planning for growth but concerned about delivery capacity, the question isn’t “who should we hire next?”

It’s “how should work move through the business?”   

Outsourcing paraplanning and CSO creates a long-term impact

Outsourcing is not just about getting through EOFY. It changes how the business operates.

Industry commentary suggests that advice practices with strong operational structures where delivery doesn’t rely on individuals and workflows are consistent, more scalable and more attractive over time.

Advice Practices that are less dependent on key individuals, maintain consistent delivery standards, and can absorb growth without disruption.

Final thoughts

The capacity challenge that Australian financial advisers are facing is real. But it isn’t solved by hiring more or faster. It’s solved by redesigning how work gets done. Because growth doesn’t come from adding more hires alone.

This is achieved by building stronger support around advisers. Outsourcing non-advice operational work to paraplanners and CSOs creates more time and flexibility, allowing advisers to focus on what matters most, clients.
